figures.evidence: Re-derived from the tree and tried to break it at the boundary between the self-test and polling. link_host.c start() refuses a request while one is pending. LINK_HOST_TIMEOUT_MS is 1000. LINK_MAX_REGS is 32 and LINK_CAN_REGS_PER_FRAME is 4, so a request is at most 8 frames. can_twai_send is called only at main.c:1663, selftest.c:33 and selftest.c:66. Probes run one at a time and are released by can_selftest_tick after 50 ms (can_selftest.c:209). The status requests of can_ask_remote are also 50 ms apart. The worst boundary case is the last probe followed by the first after-status request. They are at least about 22 ms apart: the 20 ms receive wait plus the 2 ms delay. poll_identity is 1 frame and comes at least 50 ms after the fifth status try. A sequence spaced 50 ms apart with one 22 ms gap still fits at most 9 frames in 400 ms. A 3 ms window holds at most the 8 frames of one request.

figures.evidence: The 44 + 8N data frame (Figure 2-1, printed on page 9, not page 8) and the 3-bit intermission (section 2.6, page 8) read as stated, so the classic-CAN bound of 8,511 and 64 holds. The claim 'A CAN FD frame is longer, so the bound holds for FD traffic too' is false for the traffic V20 and V21 set: CAN FD with bit-rate switching to a 5000 kbit/s data phase. CiA's CAN FD page gives the frame fields: FDF, BRS, ESI, a 3-bit Gray-coded stuff count with a parity bit and fixed stuff bits, and a 17-bit CRC for payloads up to 16 bytes, with the data-phase rate applied after BRS. An FD frame with no data then has about 30 bits at 1 Mbit/s: SOF to BRS 17, CRC delimiter, ACK, EOF 7 and IFS 3. It also has about 32 bits at 5 Mbit/s: ESI 1, DLC 4, stuff count 4, CRC 17 and 6 fixed stuff bits. That is about 36.4 us against 47 us. A saturated port can therefore deliver about 10,990 frames in 400 ms and about 83 in 3 ms. These counts are derived here and not read from a data sheet; ISO 11898-1:2015 was not read. The FD frame is longer than 47 us only without bit-rate switching.

The DroneCAN 4.4 page says DroneCAN 'operates on CANFD' and that 'frames can be up to 64 bytes'. Page 4.1 defines the classic transport. README.md:108-111 and STATUS.md:383 name DroneCAN, and no other CAN application protocol appears in the tree's .md files.

The DroneCAN section 8 table lists 1000 kbit/s as the highest recommended rate. DroneCAN 4.4 says BRS usually runs 'with a nominal bit rate of 1MBps, with payload switching to 1, 2, 4, 5 or 8 MBit depending on hardware capabilities'. SLLSFJ3D page 1 says 'to 5 megabits per second (Mbps). Up to 8Mbps operation in simpler networks'. The 5000 kbit/s figure is a choice limited by the transceivers, and it is stated as such.

The CAN bus parameters table gives these values at 1000 kbit/s: sample point 75% to 90%, recommended 87.5%, maximum bus length 40 m, maximum stub 0.3 m. The page also says the limits are 'based on the assumption that the propagation delay does not exceed 5 ns/m, not including additional delay times of CAN transceivers'.

D-Sub pin 3, CAN Ground: 'Must be interconnected with Ground (pin 6) within the device'. The M8 pinout carries Ground on pin 5, and the Micro pinout carries Ground as well. The tree states no isolation.

The D-Sub and M8 sections say: 'Devices that deliver power to the bus are required to provide 23.0-30.0 V on the bus power line, 24 V nominal'. Bus-powered devices should expect 18.0 to 30.0 V. The Micro connector gives 5.0 to 5.5 V. A CAN line shorted to bus power therefore sees up to 30.0 V.

The Micro connector section reads 'Devices that deliver power to the bus are required to provide 5.0-5.5 V'. IOBoard.md:56 gives 5 V (F6) on the link cable, and :177 says the cable carries the display's supply. The figure is taken by analogy, because the link is not a DroneCAN bus, and the answer states that.

DS20001801K section 5.6, page 43: 'A maximum node-to-node oscillator variation of 1.7% is allowed' and a quartz oscillator is required for full bus speed. AN754 page 7 gives 10tbit(A) > 10tbit(B) + tSJW(B). Tried to refute it with condition 2 of MCP25625 DS20005282C Eq. 3-7, df <= min(PHSEG1,PHSEG2)/(2(13NBT - PHSEG2)), at the link's timing. The IO board side is 8 TQ with PHSEG1 3 and PHSEG2 2 (can_timing.c:194-198), which gives 0.98%. The TWAI side is 20 TQ with PS2 5 and SJW 4, which gives 0.98% and 1.0%. The +/-0.85% taken is tighter than every condition, so the value is not weaker than its sources.

figures.evidence: The +/-0.5% input ranges read correctly: MCP2518FD Table 7-3 gives FOSC1,20M/40M at nominal -0.5% to +0.5%, and SLLSF91A says 0.5% frequency accuracy. The derivation that ±0.5% is inside what CAN allows fails. It uses only the SJW condition, 1.25% node to node at 87.5%. Microchip's condition 2, df <= min(PHSEG1,PHSEG2)/(2 x (13 x NBT - PHSEG2)) (DS20005282C Eq. 3-7), gives 0.125/(2 x 12.875) = 0.485% a node at the 87.5% sample point V27 itself uses. That is ±4,854 ppm, and it applies at any NBT. ±5,000 ppm is therefore weaker than the classic-CAN limit at that sample point, and at DroneCAN's 90% end it is 0.388%. The CAN FD data-phase tolerance conditions at 5000 kbit/s were not read from a primary source and were not evaluated. They can only tighten the limit.

figures.evidence: The drop rests on 'Holding Standby from the enable node alone needs EN and nSTB driven together, which the datasheet does not describe'. The datasheet does describe it. Figure 7-4, the state machine, gives Normal to Standby on '(EN = low and nSTB = low)' and Standby to Normal on 'EN = high and nSTB = high and VIO > UVIO'. Table 7-4 gives EN low with nSTB low as Standby for either WAKERQ state. EN and nSTB both tied to the enable node therefore give Normal while it is high and Standby while it is low. The SWE timer moves Standby to Sleep after tINACTIVE, 3 to 5 min (typical 4). The driver stays disabled in Sleep, and the next rising enable gives the low-to-high nSTB edge that Sleep needs to leave.
